A healthy antenna climbs smoothly from the horizon to zenith; a flat or dented curve points at the antenna or its siting.
Where the satellites the station tracks stand in its sky.

Each dot is a satellite the station is tracking, drawn where it stands as seen from the station: the centre is straight up, the edge is the horizon, with rings every 15° of elevation. Its colour is its constellation; its label is its PRN.

Positions come from orbits: the station’s own stream where it broadcasts them, a RINEX navigation file you import, or, in the paid edition, an ephemeris mountpoint opened while it is needed. Satellites no orbit covers are placed from this phone’s own GNSS where it sees them. The header names the source in use.

A satellite with no position is counted in the header and not drawn. An empty part of the sky is not a missing satellite.
Each line is that satellite’s track over the run.

One bar per satellite: its C/N0, the strength of its signal at the station’s receiver, in dB-Hz. The header gives the count, the mean and the range.

Means are averaged in power, not in decibels: averaging the dB numbers would understate a satellite that fades and recovers.

The station’s message type sets the resolution: MSM4 and MSM5 carry whole dB-Hz, MSM6 and MSM7 a sixteenth, MSM1 to MSM3 none at all, which leaves this screen empty. When two stations differ, compare their message types first.

Every sample of the run: a satellite’s C/N0 against its elevation at that moment, gathered into cells of one degree by one dB-Hz and coloured by constellation. The more samples in a cell, the more solid it is drawn.

A healthy installation rises smoothly from about 35 dB-Hz at the horizon to about 50 dB-Hz at zenith. A flat or dented curve points at the antenna, its siting or an obstruction rather than at the receiver.

Cells are a whole dB-Hz high because that is the coarsest any station sends; a finer grid would leave empty rows on an MSM4 station. Read the shape of the curve, not how full the cells are.

Elevation comes from the same orbits as the sky view; satellites it cannot place add nothing to the plot.
Where the station’s own GPS observations place it, against the position it broadcasts.

Each epoch is solved on its own, from GPS satellites seen on two frequencies, by the same solver the Windows GUI and the monitoring service use.\n\nThe plot is east and north around the broadcast position, which stays at the centre. The figures above it have no verdict: no threshold for a station’s own scatter has been established.

The reference position is the antenna position the stream says its corrections are for, sent in RTCM 1005/1006.

The rover is at the centre: this phone where it has a fix, otherwise the position you set. The reference position is drawn at its true bearing and distance, with where it has been this run and the distance over the last five minutes beneath.

A network service can hand you to another station as you move: that is its job. A fixed base should never move; if it does, its corrections cannot be trusted. Which of the two a mountpoint is, is decided from its sourcetable entry, the Network-RTK check’s gate test, and where its reference position stands against yours; the screen names the evidence that decided.

The caster is sent this phone’s position where you allowed it, or the position you set. With the screen off the phone’s position is not updated, so on the move the caster serves where the phone was.
Is this GNSS base station fit for RTK? Measure it, and see why.

NTRIP Analyser connects to an NTRIP caster and answers one question about a GNSS base station: is it fit to serve RTK, and if not, why?\n\nIt does not steer a rover and it does not compute a position. It measures what the station actually delivers — message types and their rates, satellites and their signal strength, the reference position it broadcasts, and how steadily it holds all of that — and states a verdict you can act on or hand to whoever runs the station.
A check ends with STATION OK, CAUTION or FAILED, and with the evidence, so the verdict can be argued with.
A check ends with STATION OK, CAUTION or FAILED; a watch adds STABLE, DEGRADED or UNSTABLE — and each comes with the evidence, so the verdict can be argued with.
Run the check: the eight checks (tier 1) — a verdict in about two minutes.
Watch station: checks plus stability (tier 2) — needs ten minutes of evidence, runs for hours.
Network-RTK check: checks plus the network at your position — answer in ~2 min, then runs until stopped.
The app is a client: it connects where you tell it to, with your own credentials. Having permission to use a caster, and observing its terms, is yours.

A run will transmit this phone’s position to %1$s about every ten seconds, so the network can serve corrections for where you are. It goes to that caster and nowhere else: this app has no server and sends nothing to its author.\n\nYou can turn this off again at any time; the position you typed is then sent instead.

Android allows about six hours of background streaming a day, and the watch reached it. What it measured up to that point is in the app.
